lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: The Lakes That Weren’t There
case.hook: A volunteer brought me three satellite photos of the same piece of central Florida, taken from space in 1985, 2004 and 2023. Dark, square lakes and bare tan patches keep showing up in new places. Lakes don’t usually come in squares! The volunteer wrote: “Lakes popping up out of nowhere?”
case.question: What is making the square lakes and bare patches, and will the thing being taken ever come back?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

stills.alt: A satellite photo of green land with a cluster of small dark squares and tan patches near the middle.
The same land in 2004. The dark squares and tan patches have spread out, mostly toward the south.
The same land in 2023. New dark squares and tan patches are near the bottom and edges. Some old spots in the middle look greener.

case.stillsCredit: Satellite photos (Landsat, 1985, 2004 and 2023) of the Bone Valley phosphate mining area southeast of Tampa Bay, from “Annual NLCD Assessment: Phosphate Mining and Land Cover Change”, U.S. Geological Survey EROS Center, 2024 (public domain). Each photo is cropped from the USGS animation.

clues.t: The fertilizer that helps Florida oranges grow starts as phosphate rock, dug out of the ground in central Florida.
Phosphate rock took millions of years to form. Once it’s dug up, it doesn’t come back, even in a million years. It’s nonrenewable.
When a mine digs out phosphate, the deep pit fills with rain and groundwater and becomes a lake. The land can be replanted, but the rock is gone.
Both sources agree: phosphate becomes fertilizer for growing food. The government report adds what the flyer left out: mines clear wetlands and fields, and leave huge waste piles.

solve.title: What is making the square lakes?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Heavy rains flooded the fields. Rain comes back, so nothing is lost.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Rain fills the pits, but what dug the square holes in the first place?

options.t: People are mining phosphate rock for fertilizer. The dug pits fill with water and become lakes. Phosphate takes millions of years to form, so it’s nonrenewable and won’t come back.
options.why: Case cracked! The square lakes are old phosphate mine pits. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: People are building solar farms, and sunlight is renewable.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 4. What do the sources say comes out of the ground there?

unmake.title: Take it apart
todo: Pick a thing: the pencil, the juice box or the orange.
Drag each of its parts to where it started on Earth, or tap the part and then the place.
Take apart all three things, then answer the question.

why.t: Anything from Earth that people use, like water, sunlight, wood or rock.

unmake.hint: Sort a part to learn more about it here.

parts.why: Most pencils are made of cedar wood. Trees can be cut and replanted.
parts.miss: Wood comes from something that grows. What is it?

parts.why: It isn’t really lead! It’s graphite, a soft gray rock, mixed with clay. Both are dug out of the ground.
parts.miss: Pencil “lead” is a soft gray rock. Where do rocks come from?

parts.why: The band that holds the eraser is aluminum. It’s made from a rock that miners dig up.
parts.miss: Metal starts as rock. Where do people get rock?

parts.why: Paper is made from wood fibers, from trees.
parts.miss: Paper is made from wood. Where does wood come from?

parts.why: Most plastic is made from oil or natural gas, pumped from deep underground.
parts.miss: Plastic is made from something pumped out of the ground. What is it?

parts.why: A thin layer of aluminum keeps the juice fresh. Aluminum starts as a rock that is mined.
parts.miss: Metal starts as rock. Where do people get rock?

parts.why: The juice comes from oranges, which grow on trees.
parts.miss: Juice comes from fruit. Where does fruit come from?

items.name: Florida orange
items.sub: What it took to grow it and get it to you:

parts.why: It grew on a tree in a Florida grove.
Rain falls again and again. Florida gets about 50 inches a year.
Leaves use sunlight to make food for the tree. The sun rises again every day.
parts.miss: Look up! Where does sunlight come from?

parts.why: Fertilizer is plant food. Much of it is made from phosphate rock, dug out of the ground in central Florida.
parts.miss: Fertilizer is made from a kind of rock. Where does rock come from?

parts.t: Fuel for the truck to the store
parts.why: Diesel fuel is made from oil, pumped from deep underground.
parts.miss: Truck fuel is made from oil. Where does oil come from?

unmake.q: Which part of the orange came out of the ground, like the pencil’s “lead”?

opts.t: The fertilizer
The rain
opts.miss: Rain falls from the sky. Which part was dug up?

opts.t: The orange itself
opts.miss: The orange grew on a tree. Which part was dug up?

unmake.win: You took everything apart! Some parts grew, some came from the sky, and some were dug up or pumped out of the ground. That’s a clue.

refill.title: Refill race
todo: Press “Use them all up”, then drag time forward. Which bars fill back up?
Try the water at both pumping speeds.
Stamp each one renewable or nonrenewable.

rows.name: Sunlight
rows.why: The sun rises again every morning.
rows.miss: Look at the sunlight bar after just 1 day. Did it come back?

rows.name: Fresh water underground
rows.why: Rain refills it every year, as long as we don’t pump faster than the rain soaks back in.
rows.miss: At the slow pumping speed, did the water come back?

rows.name: Pine forest
rows.why: New pines grow back in about 25 years, when people replant them.
rows.miss: Look at the pine bar at 25 years. Did the forest come back?

rows.name: Phosphate rock
rows.why: It took millions of years to form. Even after a million years, it isn’t back.
rows.miss: Look at the phosphate bar at 1 million years. Did it come back?

rows.name: Oil
rows.why: Oil formed from tiny sea creatures buried for millions of years.
rows.miss: Look at the oil bar at 1 million years. Did it come back?

note.slow: Pumping slower than the rain soaks back in: the water fills back up.
note.fast: Pumping faster than the rain soaks back in: the water keeps dropping, even though it’s renewable!

refill.stampQ: Stamp each one: renewable or nonrenewable?
refill.q: Dr. Reyes’s satellite photos show land being dug up for phosphate rock. Will the rock come back?

opts.t: Yes, in about a year, like rain.
opts.miss: Look at the phosphate bar at 1 year. Is it full?

opts.t: Yes, in about 25 years, like a pine forest.
opts.miss: Look at the phosphate bar at 25 years. Is it full?

opts.t: No. It takes millions of years to form, so it’s nonrenewable.

refill.win: Sunlight, water and pine forests came back. Phosphate rock and oil didn’t, not even in a million years. That’s a clue.

photos.kicker: Look closer · a real Florida phosphate mine
photos.title: How does phosphate come out of the ground?
todo: Tap each number on the photo to read what it is.
Then match the steps to the labels below.

why.t: A giant digging machine. Government scientists photographed this one at a Florida phosphate mine.

photos.alt: A giant white mining machine with a long steel arm stands behind a farm field. A bucket hangs from cables near a pale pile of sand.
photos.credit: Surface strip mining with draglines near Parrish, Florida, U.S. Geological Survey EROS Center, about 2003

hotspots.label: The dragline
hotspots.t: The giant machine. Its operator sits inside, and big motors pull the cables. It moves slowly on huge feet.

hotspots.label: The boom
hotspots.t: A long steel arm that holds the bucket far out from the machine. On the biggest draglines, it’s about as long as a football field.

hotspots.label: The bucket
hotspots.t: It hangs from cables. The dragline drops it, drags it to scoop up the ground, then lifts it and dumps it.

hotspots.label: A pile of dug-up sand
hotspots.t: First the dragline scrapes off the sand on top and piles it out of the way. The phosphate layer is under it.

hotspots.label: Land not mined yet
hotspots.t: A farm field. One dragline can dig up about 15 acres in a month, about the size of 11 football fields.

task.q: Match each step of mining to a label on the photo.
task.win: You matched every step. The phosphate comes out, and the hole it leaves becomes a pit.

items.evid: Before mining, the land was fields and wetlands.
The dragline’s long boom holds the bucket far from the machine.
The bucket scoops up the ground to reach the phosphate.

items.step: Sand moved out of the way
items.evid: Sand on top is piled to the side to reach the phosphate under it.

impact.title: Impact check
todo: Pick a photo and stamp it renewable or nonrenewable.
Pick what using it changes. Check all four photos.

cards.name: Solar farm
cards.alt: Rows and rows of dark solar panels covering a huge flat area of land, seen from the air.
cards.kindMiss: Solar panels use sunlight. Does sunlight come back?
cards.use: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity. This one at Kennedy Space Center is bigger than 350 football fields.

opts.t: It covers a lot of land, so plants and animals that lived there have to move.
It makes smoke every day.
opts.miss: Solar panels make electricity without smoke. Look at the photo: what covers the ground?

opts.t: Nothing changes, because it’s renewable.
opts.miss: Renewable means it comes back, not that nothing changes. Look at the land in the photo.

cards.fact: Solar panels make electricity with no smoke. But they need lots of land, and making them uses metals that are dug from the ground.

cards.name: Pine forest
cards.alt: Tall, straight pine trees with short palm-like plants covering the ground under them.
cards.kindMiss: Can people plant new pine trees? Do they grow back?
cards.use: People cut pines for wood and paper, then plant new ones. New pines grow back in about 25 years.
cards.q: What does cutting the forest change?

opts.t: Animals lose their homes until the new trees grow.
The trees can never grow back.
opts.miss: Pines can be replanted. How long did they take in the Refill race?

opts.t: Nothing changes, because it’s renewable.
opts.miss: Think about the animals that live in the forest. What happens to them?

cards.fact: Woodpeckers, gopher tortoises and other animals need pine forests. Foresters plant new trees and often leave some old trees standing for them.

cards.name: Oil
cards.alt: A Florida beach with brown streaks of oil washed up on the white sand.
cards.kindMiss: Oil took millions of years to form. Does it come back?
cards.use: Oil is made into gasoline and plastic. In 2010, oil from a broken well in the Gulf washed up on Pensacola Beach.

opts.t: Burning it pollutes the air, and spills hurt beaches and wildlife.
It grows back in a year.
opts.miss: Look at the oil bar in the Refill race. Did it come back?

opts.t: Nothing changes.
opts.miss: Look at the sand in the photo. What is on it?

cards.fact: Oil formed from tiny sea creatures that were buried for millions of years. Burning it for gasoline puts smoke and gases into the air.

cards.name: Phosphate mine
cards.alt: The 2023 satellite photo: green land with dark square lakes and bare tan patches.
cards.kindMiss: Phosphate rock took millions of years to form. Does it come back?
cards.use: Draglines dig up phosphate rock to make fertilizer. This is the 2023 satellite photo from the case file.

opts.t: The land is dug into deep pits, and the pits fill with water and become lakes.
It fills the air with smoke, like burning oil.
opts.miss: Look at the photo. What do you see on the land?

opts.t: Nothing changes.
opts.miss: Look at the dark squares in the photo. What are they?

cards.fact: Rain and groundwater fill the empty pits, making square lakes. Since 1975, Florida law has said mined land must be fixed up afterward, with new plants and shaped lakes. But the phosphate rock is gone for good.

impact.q: A classmate says, “Renewable means no impact.” What did you find?

opts.t: All four changed something. Renewables still have impacts, but sunlight and trees come back.
Only the nonrenewable ones had an impact.
opts.miss: Look back at the solar farm and the pine forest. Did they change anything?

opts.t: None of them had an impact.
opts.miss: Look at the oil on the beach and the pits in the land.

impact.credit: Solar farm: Discovery Solar Energy Center at NASA Kennedy Space Center, NASA, 2021, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Pine forest: Longleaf pine forest, Osceola National Forest, Florida, Geoff Gallice, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0). Oil: Oil-stained beach in Pensacola, Florida, July 1, 2010, Geoff Livingston, via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0). Mine: Satellite photos (Landsat, 1985, 2004 and 2023) of the Bone Valley phosphate mining area southeast of Tampa Bay, from “Annual NLCD Assessment: Phosphate Mining and Land Cover Change”, U.S. Geological Survey EROS Center, 2024 (public domain).
impact.win: Every resource has an impact, even renewable ones. The square lakes in the case are mine pits filled with water. That’s a clue.

twosources.afterText: Dr. Reyes found two sources about the phosphate mines
twosources.title: Two sources, one claim
todo: Drag each fact to Benefit or Cost, or tap the fact and then the box.
Answer three questions to build a fair claim.

sources.by: A flyer from a mining company (a pretend company for this case)

facts.t: Florida phosphate helps make fertilizer that farmers use to grow food.
Mining gives jobs to many people in central Florida.
When we finish digging, we replant the land and shape lakes and fields.
facts.miss: Fixing up the land helps. Is that a benefit or a cost?

sources.t: Phosphate Mining and Land Cover Change
sources.by: A report by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), a team of government scientists, 2024
sources.alt: A huge pale gray hill of waste with a bulldozer and a digger parked on top.

facts.t: Mines clear away wetlands, grassland and pasture to dig the phosphate.
Making fertilizer leaves giant waste piles, like the one in the photo. Florida has about 1 billion tons of this waste.
About 95 out of every 100 tons of U.S. phosphate rock is used for fertilizer and animal food.
facts.miss: Fertilizer grows food for people. Is that a benefit or a cost?

bins.t: Cost: it harms land, water or wildlife

steps.q: Which fact is ONLY in Source B?

opts.t: Mines clear away wetlands, grassland and pasture.
Phosphate is used to make fertilizer.
opts.miss: Both sources say that one. Which fact did the flyer leave out?

opts.t: Mining gives jobs.
opts.miss: That’s in the flyer, Source A.

steps.q: What do BOTH sources agree on?

opts.t: Phosphate rock is used to make fertilizer that grows food.
Mining doesn’t change the land.
opts.miss: Does Source B say that? Look at its facts.

opts.t: Florida has giant waste piles.
opts.miss: Only Source B says that.

steps.q: Which claim is fair to BOTH sources?

opts.t: Phosphate mining is all good.
opts.miss: That only uses Source A. What did Source B add?

opts.t: Phosphate mining helps grow food, but it clears land and leaves waste, and the rock won’t come back.
Phosphate mining is all bad.
opts.miss: That only uses Source B. What benefit do both sources agree on?

twosources.credit: Source A is a pretend flyer made for this case. Source B facts: A stack of phosphogypsum in Florida and the USGS EROS Center report “Annual NLCD Assessment: Phosphate Mining and Land Cover Change” (2024). Photo: A stack of phosphogypsum in Florida, U.S. Geological Survey EROS Center, about 2003 (public domain).
twosources.win: You used two sources to make a fair claim! One source alone would have told only half the story. That’s your last clue.

q1.A: Oil took millions of years to form. Is it back by tomorrow?
q1.C: Limestone formed slowly under ancient seas. What comes back every day?

q2.A: Being hard to find isn’t the reason. Think about the Refill race: how long did they take?
q2.B: Price isn’t the reason. Think about time.

q3.A: Think about the solar farm in Impact check. Did it change the land?
q3.C: Solar panels make no smoke. Which has the bigger impact: solar or oil?

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: A solar farm is renewable, but it covers a lot of land where animals lived.
Pine forests grow back, but animals lose their homes until new trees grow.
Phosphate is nonrenewable, but it makes fertilizer that helps grow food.
Oil spills hurt beaches and wildlife, and burning oil pollutes the air.
Every resource in Impact check changed the land, air, water or wildlife.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · the lakes that weren’t there
welcome.script: Hi, it’s Dr. Reyes. A volunteer brought me three photos taken from space: the same piece of central Florida in 1985, 2004 and 2023. See the dark square lakes and the bare tan patches? They keep showing up in new places. Lakes don’t usually come in squares. What is making them? And is something being taken that won’t come back? Let’s find four clues.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · take it apart (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Everything you use started somewhere on Earth. Pick the pencil, the juice box or the orange, and take it apart. Drag each part to where it started. Did it grow? Did it come from the sky? Or did it come out of the ground? Save the orange for last. It has a surprise inside.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. Hold up something renewable (a leaf) and something nonrenewable (a rock or a plastic bottle).

part1.label: Part 1 · what counts as a resource

part2.label: Part 2 · refill race (Clue 2)
part2.script: Time for a race! Press the button to use up all five resources. Then drag time forward: one day, one year, all the way to a million years. Watch the bars. Which ones fill back up? And try the water at both pumping speeds. Something sneaky happens when you pump fast.

part3.label: Part 3 · impact check (Clue 3)
part3.script: Even good choices change things. Open each photo. First, stamp it renewable or nonrenewable. Then pick what using it changes. Here’s my hint: none of them gets “nothing changes.” And look closely at the mine photo. Does it look familiar?

explore.label: Part 4 · two sources (Clue 4)
explore.script: Two sources, one claim. A mining company made Source A. Government scientists wrote Source B. Sort every fact: is it a benefit or a cost? Then find what one source left out. When you can make a claim that’s fair to both, you’ll have your last clue.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what is making those square lakes, and will it come back? Then answer two questions, compare two Florida resources in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says all renewable resources are good for the environment, and all nonrenewable ones are bad. Hmm. Think about the solar farm and the phosphate mine. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! The square lakes are old phosphate mine pits. The rock became fertilizer, and it won’t come back. Next time, we’ll read a map of Florida. Why is phosphate found in just one part of the state? Bring your detective eyes.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain which resources come back and which run out?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Phosphate rock takes millions of years to form, so it is nonrenewable.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “phosphate rock”, “millions of years” and “nonrenewable”. Those words tell what it is and why. Small words like “of” and “so” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

tool.name: Core drill
tool.teaser: Drill into the ground at three Florida spots, pull up the layers, and find where the phosphate is.
tool.done: You drilled three spots and read the layers like a geologist. A core drill sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A drill with a hollow bit. As it spins down into the ground, a long column of soil and rock slides up inside it. Scientists pull it out to see the layers.

coredrill.title: What’s under Florida?
todo: Tap each part of the core drill to learn it.
Pick a spot, then press Drill. Drill all three spots.
Tap the layers in your cores to read them, then answer the question.

parts.label: The hollow drill bit
parts.t: Its sharp teeth cut a round hole. The middle is empty, so a column of ground slides up inside.

parts.label: The core tube
parts.t: The long tube that holds the sample as the drill goes deeper.

parts.label: The core box
parts.t: Scientists lay each sample in a long box, top at the top, so they can read the layers in order.

sites.name: Central Florida
sites.where: A pasture near Bone Valley, east of Tampa

layers.note: Loose sand on top. Miners call it the overburden (the layer over the good stuff) and pile it to the side first.
Gray-brown pebbles mixed with sand and clay. They formed millions of years ago, when shallow seas covered this part of Florida. Fossil shark teeth are found in this layer!
Rock made from the shells and skeletons of ancient sea life. Florida’s underground fresh water fills its tiny holes.

sites.name: South Florida
sites.where: Near Miami, at the edge of the Everglades

layers.note: Only a few inches to a few feet of soil here. Rock is right under your feet.
This limestone is dug up to make cement and roads. Water seeps into the pits, so they turn into lakes. No phosphate layer here.

sites.name: North Florida
sites.where: Near the springs north of Gainesville

layers.note: Rain soaks down through this sand.
This is the Floridan Aquifer, an underground layer of rock that holds fresh water. Springs bubble out of it. Most Floridians get their drinking water from underground.

q.q: Where would a mining company drill to find phosphate?

opts.t: Central Florida
opts.why: Yes! Only the central Florida core had a phosphate layer. Next lesson, a map of Florida will show you why.

opts.t: South Florida
opts.why: Look at the South Florida core. Is there a phosphate layer?

opts.t: North Florida
opts.why: Look at the North Florida core. Is there a phosphate layer?
